C0.quote: we consider two fundamental social choice problems: single-winner voting and one-sided matching
C0.note: Single-winner voting is a main object. One-sided matching is a second setting studied in the same distortion framework.

C1.quote: We show tight tradeoﬀs between the consistency and robustness of ordinal mechanisms
C1.note: All main results are consistency and robustness bounds on distortion, i.e. welfare ratios. The polynomial-time remark in Lemma 4.1 is auxiliary and not a main algorithmic result.

C2.1.value: ordinal profile / ordinal preferences (reported ordering or ranking), plus predicted valuation profile (prediction information p)
C2.1.quote: each voter i reports an ordering (or, ranking) ≻vi of the candidates

C2.2.quote: some (partial) valuation proﬁle v̂ which also induces the same ordinal proﬁle
C2.2.note: The mechanism's argument is the ordinal ranking profile plus a prediction p. In most results p is a (partial) cardinal valuation profile (CARD). In Theorem 3.1, p is a predicted optimal candidate (OTH: predicted outcome).

C2.3.quote: Each voter i ∈ N has a valuation function vi : A → R≥0

C2.4.quote: be the ordinal proﬁle of the voters induced by v
C2.4.note: Separate notation for true valuations v, induced ranking ≻v, and predicted valuations v̂. The text says the prediction may differ from the true values.

C3.1.quote: each voter i reports an ordering (or, ranking) ≻vi of the candidates
C3.1.note: Prediction errors are not modelled as strategic misreporting by voters.

C3.2.quote: such that x ≻vi y implies vi (x) ≥ vi (y)
C3.2.note: Reported rankings are stated to be consistent with the true valuations.

C3.3.note: The intro motivates ordinal elicitation by cognitive ease, but gives no reason why reports are truthful.

C4.1.quote: such that x ≻vi y implies vi (x) ≥ vi (y)
C4.1.note: Utilities are consistent with the ranking, with unit-sum normalization.

C5.1.quote: The distortion is a measure of the loss in social welfare

C5.2.note: Welfare is evaluated on the true valuations v, which are separate from the ordinal input and the prediction.

VOT.quote_behav: each voter i reports an ordering (or, ranking) ≻vi of the candidates
VOT.note: Voters take a fixed action in the model by reporting rankings consistent with their valuations. Agents in one-sided matching are treated the same way.

claims.quote: The goal is to leverage the prediction to achieve improved distortion guarantees
the main takeaway message is that improved distortion guarantees can be achieved
depending on how much the prediction can be trusted

C9.1.note: These are claims about welfare guarantees and about choosing mechanism parameters.

C9.2.quote: such that x ≻vi y implies vi (x) ≥ vi (y)
C9.2.note: Needed assumptions are all stated: rankings consistent with true valuations, unit-sum normalization, and non-strategic reporting of rankings.

C1.reason: The main results are distortion (welfare-ratio) bounds and computation is not studied as a main result, so AL does not apply.

C2.2.reason: The rule's argument includes the predicted valuations, as A codes, and in the main Theorem 3.1 also a predicted optimal candidate, which needs OTH.

C6.VOT.reason: Under C6, an agent taking a fixed action counts as present, and voters are explicitly said to report rankings, so they are present and non-strategic.
